teile.einleitung: The honey bee is an insect that lives in large communities, the bee colonies. It makes honey and wax and pollinates many plants, which is why it is very important for nature and farming.
wichtigste: Every bee colony has a queen, who lays all the eggs.
The worker bees are female and do almost all the jobs.
The male bees are called drones.
Bees show the way to flowers with a dance.
A honey bee has five eyes.
When it stings a person’s skin, the sting is often left behind.

abschnitte.text: A bee colony consists of a **queen**, many **worker bees** and, in summer, also **drones**. The queen is the largest bee and lays all the **eggs**. The workers are females. The drones are the male bees. They have no sting and do not collect nectar. In summer a colony can have many thousands of bees.

The **worker bees** have many jobs. They clean the cells, feed the larvae and build **honeycombs** from wax. Later they guard the entrance. Last of all they fly out and collect **nectar** and **pollen**. In doing so, they carry pollen from flower to flower. In this way they **pollinate** many fruit trees and other plants.

When a forager has found good flowers, she flies back to the hive. There she **dances** on the comb. With the dance she shows the other bees the **direction** and the **distance** to the flowers. If the flowers are further away, she does a **waggle dance**. The researcher Karl von Frisch decoded this bee language.

A honey bee has **five eyes**. Two large **compound eyes** sit at the sides of the head. In addition there are three small **simple eyes** on top of the head. The worker’s **sting** has small **barbs**. If she stings a person, it stays stuck in the skin and tears off. That is why the bee usually dies afterwards.

gewusst: For one jar of honey, bees together fly a very long way and visit millions of flowers.
Karl von Frisch received the Nobel Prize in 1973 for his research on bee language.

teile.einleitung: In integrated pest management, farmers protect their plants with many different means. Chemical sprays are used only when it is really necessary.
wichtigste: Preventive measures come first, chemical products only as much as necessary.
Control starts only once the economic damage threshold is reached.
A varied crop rotation keeps disease organisms in the soil low.
Forecasting models such as Agrometeo show the right time for a treatment.
Flower strips encourage beneficial insects such as hoverflies and lacewings.
Changing active ingredients prevents resistance.

abschnitte.titel: Prevention is the most important thing
abschnitte.text: The principle is: **preventive measures first**, chemical products only as much as necessary. These include robust varieties, healthy soil and a **varied crop rotation**. If something different grows in a field each year, disease organisms in the soil cannot build up as strongly. They then do not always find their favourite plant in the same place.

Not every pest is a problem straight away. First you count and observe. Only when the infestation goes above the **economic damage threshold** is control worthwhile. Then the damage would be greater than the cost of the treatment. **Pheromone traps** help with this: they use scents to attract certain moths and show when these are flying.

In Switzerland, many farmers and winegrowers use the **Agrometeo** platform. It uses weather data to calculate when, for example, a fungus could attack the vines. With such **forecasting models**, spraying is done only when it is really necessary. This saves products and protects the environment.

**Flower strips** are laid out at the edge of fields. They encourage **beneficial insects** such as hoverflies, lacewings and ladybirds, whose larvae eat aphids. In Swiss viticulture, the **confusion technique** is used against the **grape berry moth**. In it, many scents of the females are spread around in the vines. The males therefore cannot find the females, and there are fewer caterpillars.

If the same product is always sprayed, a few disease organisms that are insensitive sometimes survive. They multiply, and the product no longer works. This is called **resistance**. That is why people alternate between **active ingredients with different modes of action**.

gewusst: With the confusion technique, small scent dispensers hang in the vines, with no poison at all.
A single lacewing larva can eat a great many aphids in its life.

teile.einleitung: An insect hotel is a nesting aid for wild bees and other insects. You can build one yourself and put it in the garden or on the balcony.
wichtigste: An insect hotel is a nesting aid.
It should stand in a sunny spot.
A roof protects it from rain.
Hollow bamboo tubes and holes in hard wood are good nesting places.
The holes must be smooth inside and free of splinters.
Mason bees especially like to move in.

abschnitte.text: Many wild bees live alone and lay their eggs in small hollow spaces. In tidy gardens they often find no such places. An **insect hotel** is a **nesting aid**: it offers many small tubes. The bee puts pollen in as food and lays an egg, then seals the chamber. The next spring a new bee hatches.

Insects love warmth. That is why the insect hotel should face **the sun**, ideally south or south-east. A **roof** protects it **from rain**, because wet tubes can go mouldy. The hotel should stand firmly and not sway in the wind. Very important: nearby there must be **plenty of flowers**, otherwise the bees find no food.

**Hollow bamboo tubes** or reed stems are well suited. You can also drill holes **in hard wood**, for example in beech or ash. The holes should be of different widths. It is important that they are **smooth and free of splinters** inside, otherwise the bees hurt their wings. Pine cones and loose straw are hardly used by wild bees.

**Mason bees** especially like to move in. They seal their tubes with clay. Other species use pieces of leaf or resin. From the sealed entrance you can tell that a tube is occupied. Wild bees are peaceful and hardly ever sting, so you can watch them from close by.

gewusst: Many wild bees fly only a few hundred metres, which is why flowers must be close by.
Some of the wild bees nest in the ground and need open, sandy spots instead of tubes.

teile.einleitung: The dog rose is the most common wild rose here. It grows in hedges and at the edge of woods, blooms pale pink in early summer and bears red fruits in autumn, the rose hips.
wichtigste: The dog rose is a wild rose.
It is also called the hedge rose.
It blooms mainly in June.
Its flowers are light pink to white and have five petals.
Its shoots bear curved prickles.
Its fruits contain a lot of vitamin C and make tea.

abschnitte.text: The **dog rose** grows wild in **hedges**, at the **edges of woods** and along paths. That is why it is also called the **hedge rose**. It is the most common **wild rose** here. The shrub can grow several metres tall. Its long shoots often bend downwards in an arch.

The dog rose blooms in **early summer**, mainly in **June**. Its flowers are **pale pink to white** and have a light scent. As with other wild roses, they have only **five petals**. In the middle sit many yellow stamens. Bees and bumblebees like to visit the flowers.

The shoots of the dog rose bear curved **prickles**. With them it holds on to other plants and climbs upwards. Strictly speaking, these are prickles and not thorns, because they sit only on the bark and can be broken off easily. In the dense thicket, birds find shelter and build their nests.

After the flowering, the red fruits form, the **rose hips**. They contain a lot of **vitamin C**, often more than lemons. Dried, they make a red, slightly sour **tea**. You can also make jam or purée from them. In winter, rose hips are food for birds.

gewusst: The seeds inside the rose hip are surrounded by fine hairs that children used to use as itching powder.
Many garden roses are grafted onto dog rose roots, because these are very robust.

teile.einleitung: A legume is a special kind of fruit that you know from peas and beans. Many legumes are important foods because they contain a lot of protein.
wichtigste: A pod is a fruit that opens along two seams when ripe.
Pods are typical of the legume plant family.
Peas, beans, lentils, chickpeas and soya beans are legumes.
The peanut is also a legume, and its fruits ripen in the ground.
Siliques, as in rape and mustard, have a partition in the middle.
Tofu is made from soya beans, and hummus from chickpeas.

abschnitte.text: A **pod** forms from a single carpel. The seeds sit in a row along the seam. When the pod becomes ripe and dry, it opens along **two seams**, the ventral seam and the dorsal seam. In some species the two halves spring open so forcefully that the seeds are flung away. Anyone who opens a pea pod sees the seeds neatly lined up.

Plants with pods belong to the **legume family**, one of the largest plant families. It includes pea, bean, lentil, clover and also trees such as the false acacia. Many have small nodules on their roots with **nodule bacteria**. These take nitrogen from the air and make it usable for the plant. That is why legumes improve the soil.

abschnitte.titel: The peanut, a bean in the ground
abschnitte.text: Despite its name, the **peanut** is not a true nut but a legume. After flowering, a stalk grows downwards into the earth. There the pods ripen in the ground. The net-like shell that you break when cracking it open is the pod.

In everyday speech people often say “pea pod” for any such fruit, but in botany a pod and a silique are different things. True **siliques** are formed, for example, by rape and mustard. They arise from two carpels and have a thin **partition** in the middle. When one opens, the two valves come away, and the partition with the seeds stays standing.

Legumes are rich in **protein** and fibre. **Soya beans** are made into tofu and soya milk. **Chickpeas** are used to make hummus. The **runner bean**, with its bright red flowers, grows in many gardens. Raw beans are poisonous, and you must always cook them well.

gewusst: The peanut pushes its young fruits into the earth itself so that they ripen there.
Thanks to nodule bacteria, legumes need less nitrogen fertiliser.

teile.einleitung: Jan Ingenhousz was a doctor and naturalist of the 18th century. He discovered that plants give off oxygen only in light, and so laid a foundation for the understanding of photosynthesis.
wichtigste: Jan Ingenhousz came from the Netherlands.
He was a doctor by profession.
He discovered that plants give off oxygen only in light.
Only the green parts of plants give off oxygen.
In 1779 his book “Experiments upon Vegetables” appeared.
He was friends with Benjamin Franklin.

abschnitte.text: Jan Ingenhousz was born in **1730** in Breda in the **Netherlands**. He studied medicine and worked as a **doctor**. Later he lived in England. There he learned about a method of protecting people against **smallpox**. At that time smallpox was a very dangerous disease.

In **1768** Ingenhousz travelled to **Vienna**. There he protected members of the imperial family of Maria Theresa against smallpox. The success made him famous, and he became personal physician at the court. Besides medicine, he worked on many scientific questions, such as electricity and plants.

Ingenhousz put plants under water and observed small bubbles of gas. He found that plants improve the air and give off **oxygen**, but **only in light**. And only the **green parts** do this. In the **shade** or at **night**, by contrast, plants make the air worse. Today we know that in light, green plants carry out **photosynthesis**, but they always have to breathe.

He published his results in **1779** in the book **“Experiments upon Vegetables”**. In it he built on the experiments of the Englishman Joseph Priestley. Ingenhousz was good friends with the American scientist and statesman **Benjamin Franklin**. The two wrote each other many letters about their research.

gewusst: As early as 1785, Ingenhousz observed the trembling movement of tiny specks of charcoal in alcohol, long before it could be explained.
That plants make the air worse in the dark is due to their breathing, which goes on day and night.

teile.einleitung: The timber stock is the total amount of wood contained in the living trees of a forest. Switzerland measures it regularly with the National Forest Inventory and therefore knows exactly how much wood grows back and is used.
wichtigste: The National Forest Inventory (NFI) records the condition of the Swiss forest.
In the survey of 2018 to 2022, the timber stock was around 420 million cubic metres.
The spruce has the largest share of the stock, at around 42 per cent.
On the Central Plateau, the share of spruce is falling because of drought, storms and bark beetles.
Hans Carl von Carlowitz set out the idea of sustainability in 1713.
The Forest Police Act of 1876 laid the foundation for forest protection in Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: How much wood stands in the forest?
abschnitte.text: The **National Forest Inventory**, or **NFI** for short, measures the Swiss forest on many sample plots. In the survey of 2018 to 2022, it found around **420 million cubic metres** of wood in living trees. This makes the Swiss forest one of the **richest in timber stock** in Europe. For a single piece of forest, you work it out like this: 12 hectares with 350 cubic metres each give 4,200 cubic metres of timber stock.

According to the 2025 forest report, around **42 per cent** of the stock is **spruce**. It used to be planted a lot because it grows quickly and supplies good building timber. On the warm, low-lying **Central Plateau**, however, the shallow-rooted spruce suffers from **heat and drought**. Weakened trees are easily attacked by **bark beetles** or blown over by storms. That is why their share is falling there, and broadleaved trees are becoming more important.

According to the NFI, around **10.6 million cubic metres** of wood grow each year in gross terms. After deducting the trees that die naturally, around 8.0 million remain in net terms. So around 2.6 million cubic metres die, and they often stay in the forest as **deadwood**. Around 7.1 million cubic metres are used, which is about **67 per cent** of the gross growth. So less wood is harvested than grows back.

In 1713, the Saxon chief mining officer **Hans Carl von Carlowitz** wrote the book “Sylvicultura oeconomica”. He demanded that no more wood be cut than grows back. He is regarded as the originator of the term **sustainability**. In Switzerland, clear-cutting and major floods led to the **Forest Police Act of 1876**. It first applied to the high mountains and was later extended to the whole of Switzerland.

gewusst: Deadwood is not waste: many beetles, fungi and birds depend on it.
The word sustainability, which is used everywhere today, originally comes from forestry.

teile.einleitung: Why do many animal species live on some islands and only a few on others? The theory of island biogeography gives an answer. Today it is important for nature conservation too.
wichtigste: Robert MacArthur and Edward O. Wilson published the theory in 1967.
The number of species comes from a balance between immigration and extinction.
On large islands, fewer species die out than on small ones.
The further an island is from the mainland, the fewer species arrive.
Even at equilibrium, species keep changing.
Krakatau is regarded as an open-air laboratory of recolonisation.

abschnitte.text: In **1967**, **Robert MacArthur** and **Edward O. Wilson** published the theory of **island biogeography**. It says: on an island, new species keep arriving, while others die out. The number of species settles at a **balance** between **immigration** and **extinction**. Even then, which species are present keeps changing. This exchange is called **species turnover**.

On **large islands** there are more habitats and larger populations. That is why the **extinction rate is lower**, and more species live there. If an island lies **far from the mainland**, fewer animals and seeds reach it. The **immigration rate falls**. Mathematically, the relationship is described by S = c · A to the power z. With z = 0.3, the number of species grows by about a **factor of 2** when the area becomes ten times larger.

In the 1960s, **Daniel Simberloff** and Edward O. Wilson carried out a famous experiment. On small **mangrove islands** in Florida, they removed all the **arthropods**, that is, insects, spiders and their relatives. Then they observed how the islands were colonised again. A natural example is the volcanic island of **Krakatau**. After the enormous eruption of **1883**, almost all life there was wiped out, and researchers followed how plants and animals returned.

The theory does not apply only to islands in the sea. A wood between fields, a mountain lake or a **protected area** is also a kind of island. In the **SLOSS debate**, people ask whether **one large or several small protected areas** are better. Many experts today stress that protected areas should also be well **connected**, so that animals and plants can get from one to another. This applies in densely used Switzerland too.

gewusst: SLOSS is an English abbreviation for “single large or several small”.
On Krakatau, the first plants were growing again only a few years after the eruption.

teile.einleitung: Bumblebees are round, furry insects that belong to the bees. They fly even in cool weather and are therefore important pollinators in spring and in the mountains.
wichtigste: Bumblebees belong to the bees.
Their bodies are round and densely hairy.
They fly even in cool weather.
Only the young queens survive the winter.
Many bumblebees nest in holes in the ground.
A bumblebee colony is much smaller than a honey bee colony.

abschnitte.text: Bumblebees are a group of **bees**. Like other bees, they collect **nectar** and **pollen**. Their bodies are **round** and have a thick **fur**. The fur keeps them warm. When they fly, their wings beat fast, which makes a **deep buzzing**. Bumblebees are peaceful and only very rarely sting.

Honey bees often stay in the hive in cool weather. Bumblebees fly anyway. They **shiver** with their **flight muscles** and warm themselves up that way. That is why they are out and about early in spring. They visit flowers high up in the **mountains** and in rainy weather too.

Many bumblebees build their nest in **holes in the ground**, for example in old **mouse holes**. A bumblebee colony usually has only **a few hundred** animals, while a bee colony is much bigger. In autumn the bumblebee colony dies. Only the **young queens** hibernate, often in the soil. In spring each of them founds a new colony.

Bumblebees can shake flowers with **vibrations**. This makes the pollen fall out. It works especially well with **tomato flowers**. That is why vegetable growers use bumblebees in the **greenhouse**. This means more tomatoes form. For this, bumblebee colonies are specially bred and delivered in cardboard boxes.

gewusst: Several dozen different species of bumblebee live in Switzerland.
By shivering, bumblebees can raise their body temperature to over 30 degrees, even when it is cool outside.

teile.einleitung: The Japanese beetle is a small, shimmering beetle that originally comes from Japan. It eats a great many different plants and counts in Switzerland as a dangerous pest that must be reported.
wichtigste: The scientific name is Popillia japonica.
In Switzerland it was first found in 2017, in Ticino.
It has a green head, copper-brown wing cases and white tufts of hair.
The larvae eat the roots of lawns and meadows.
The beetles eat leaves until only the veins are left.
Finds outside known areas are reported to the cantonal plant protection service.

abschnitte.text: The **Japanese beetle** is called **Popillia japonica** in scientific terms. It is about 1 centimetre long. Its head and thorax shine **metallic green**, and the wing cases are **copper-brown**. Typical are the **white tufts of hair** at the sides and at the end of the abdomen. This is how it is told apart from the similar native **garden chafer**, which lacks these tufts.

The Japanese beetle is not fussy. It eats hundreds of plant species, for example vines, fruit trees, roses and maize. The beetles eat the leaves so that only the **leaf veins** are left. This is called **skeletonising**. The **larvae** live in the soil and eat the **roots of lawns and meadows**. Then the grass turns brown and can be lifted off like a carpet.

At the beginning of the 20th century, the beetle was brought into the **USA**. There it caused great damage. Later it reached Europe. In Switzerland it was first discovered in **2017** in **Ticino**. It counts as a **quarantine organism**. This means that its spread must be prevented by all means.

In infested zones, special rules apply. At times it is forbidden to **water lawns**. The eggs and larvae need **damp soil**, and in dry soil they survive less well. Anyone who finds a Japanese beetle **outside known infested areas** should catch it, photograph it and report it to the **cantonal plant protection service**.

gewusst: A Japanese beetle can travel long distances as a stowaway by car, by train or in deliveries of plants.
The larvae are white, curved grubs that spend the winter in the soil.

teile.einleitung: Ingo Potrykus is a plant biologist from Germany who did research in Switzerland for a long time. He became known for Golden Rice, a genetically modified variety of rice against vitamin A deficiency.
wichtigste: Ingo Potrykus comes from Germany and did research in Switzerland for a long time.
From 1976 he built up a research group at the Friedrich Miescher Institute in Basel.
At ETH Zurich he developed Golden Rice with Peter Beyer.
In 2000 the work was published in the journal “Science”.
Poor farmers were to be allowed to use the rice free of charge under humanitarian licences.
Golden Rice is still controversial today.

abschnitte.titel: From the Basel laboratory to ETH
abschnitte.text: Ingo Potrykus was born in **Germany**. From **1976** he built up a research group for **plant genetic engineering** at the **Friedrich Miescher Institute** in Basel. Later he became professor of plant sciences at **ETH Zurich**. There he worked on how crop plants can be given new characteristics.

In many poor countries, people eat almost nothing but rice. They often lack **vitamin A**, which can lead to eyesight problems and illness. Together with **Peter Beyer** from Freiburg im Breisgau, Potrykus developed a rice that makes **beta-carotene** in the grain. The body turns this into vitamin A. The beta-carotene colours the grains yellowish, hence the name **Golden Rice**. In **2000** they presented their work in the journal “Science”.

Potrykus wanted the rice to help people in need. Poor farmers were to be allowed to grow it **free of charge** under **humanitarian licences**. To promote its spread, he chaired the **Golden Rice Humanitarian Board**. This body works with research institutes in Asia.

There is a long debate about Golden Rice. **Critics** doubt its usefulness and reject genetically modified plants. They propose fighting vitamin A deficiency with a varied diet or vitamin tablets. Potrykus argued, on the other hand, that very **strict regulation** delays help for people with vitamin A deficiency. In Switzerland, the growing of genetically modified plants has been severely restricted by a moratorium since a popular vote in 2005.

gewusst: The colour of Golden Rice comes from the same substance that also makes carrots orange.
Around two decades passed from the first publication to approval in a country.

teile.einleitung: A hydrophyte is an aquatic plant that lives wholly or partly in water. Such plants have special body plans so that they can float, breathe and take up nutrients.
wichtigste: Hydrophytes grow submerged, floating or with floating leaves.
Air-filled cavities, the aerenchyma, provide buoyancy and gas exchange.
In floating leaves, the stomata are on the upper side.
Submerged leaves often have only a thin cuticle.
Many water plants overwinter as winter buds on the bottom.
Canadian waterweed from North America has spread widely in Swiss waters.

abschnitte.text: Many water plants have large, **air-filled cavities** in their stems and leaves. This tissue is called **aerenchyma**. It gives **buoyancy**, so that leaves and stems float. It also carries **oxygen** down to the roots in the muddy ground. There, there is hardly any oxygen otherwise.

With **floating leaves**, such as those of the **water lily**, the underside lies on the water. That is why the **stomata** for gas exchange sit on the **upper side**. Submerged leaves often have only a very thin **cuticle**, that is, a layer of wax. Under water there is no danger of drying out. The plant takes up gases, water and nutrients directly through its whole surface.

The **water crowfoot** forms finely divided leaves under water, which offer little resistance to the current. Above water it has broad, lobed floating leaves. Different leaf shapes on one plant are called **heterophylly**. Many water plants such as the **bladderwort** form compact **winter buds** in autumn, called **turions**. They sink to the bottom and sprout again in spring.

On the shore of a lake, plants follow one another in zones. From deep water towards the land, there is first the **submerged leaf zone**, then the **floating leaf zone** and after that the **reedbed** with reeds. Further towards the land come **sedges** and fen woodland. This sequence also shows how a lake slowly **silts up**. In Switzerland, **Canadian waterweed** from North America has spread widely. As an invasive neophyte, it can form dense stands and push out native species.

gewusst: The giant water lily Victoria amazonica from the Amazon basin has leaves more than two metres across, which can bear great weight thanks to ribs on the underside.
Hydrophyte literally means “water plant”, from the Greek hydor for water and phyton for plant.

teile.einleitung: IP-Suisse is an association of farmers in Switzerland. Its label with the ladybird stands for food that is produced in an especially environmentally friendly and animal-friendly way.
wichtigste: IP-Suisse is an association of Swiss farmers.
“IP” stands for “integrated production”.
The label shows a ladybird.
The farms must give special support to biodiversity.
For cereals, they do without insecticides and fungicides.
For animals, especially animal-friendly keeping with outdoor access applies.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who sees a **ladybird** on bread, flour, meat or potatoes in a shop has a product from IP-Suisse in front of them. The ladybird fits well: it eats aphids and is a well-known **beneficial insect**. It shows that nature helps to keep the plants healthy. Many of these products can be bought in large Swiss shops.

**Integrated production** means: as little chemistry as necessary. First, preventive measures, robust varieties and beneficial insects are relied on. Unlike in **organic farming**, synthetic sprays may be used in a targeted way, but only if it is really necessary. For cereals such as wheat, IP-Suisse farmers do without **insecticides** against insects and **fungicides** against fungi.

IP-Suisse farms must give special support to **biodiversity**, that is, the variety of plants and animals. To do this they collect points with measures such as hedges, flower meadows, piles of stones or nesting places. That way insects, birds and small mammals find food and shelter in the middle of farmland.

For animals, too, strict rules apply. They are to be kept in an **especially animal-friendly** way, with enough space in the barn and regular **outdoor access**. Cows, pigs and hens can then move around more and show their natural behaviour.

gewusst: The ladybird on the label is a beneficial insect that eats aphids.
Integrated production lies between conventional farming and organic farming.

teile.einleitung: A hypha is a fine fungal thread. What we see in the woods as a mushroom is only a small part. Most of the fungus lives invisibly in the soil or in wood as a network of hyphae.
wichtigste: Fungi consist of microscopically thin threads, the hyphae.
Hyphae grow at their tip.
The mesh of many hyphae is called a mycelium.
In mycorrhiza, fungi and trees exchange substances.
Hyphae digest their food outside the fungus.
A dark honey fungus in Oregon is regarded as one of the largest living things on Earth.

abschnitte.text: Fungi consist of microscopically thin threads, the **hyphae**. Many hyphae together form a mesh, the **mycelium**. It runs through the soil, leaf litter or wood. The mushroom that we pick is only the **fruiting body**. Hyphae grow longer at their **tip**. In this way they can work their way purposefully through soil or wood.

Fungi cannot carry out photosynthesis. They have to take in their food. To do this, the hyphae give off **enzymes**, that is, digestive substances. These break down the food **outside** the fungus. The hyphae then absorb the dissolved building blocks through their surface. In this way many fungi break down dead wood and leaves and help to form humus.

Many fungi live with trees in a **partnership**, the **mycorrhiza**. The hyphae wrap around the fine tree roots. The tree gives the fungus **sugar** that it has made by photosynthesis. The fungus supplies the tree with **water and mineral salts**. Its fine network reaches much further into the soil than the roots do. Because hyphae can connect several trees, people jokingly speak of the **“Wood Wide Web”**.

Some fungi attack living trees and harm them. Such fungi are called **parasites**. They draw nutrients from their host and weaken it. One example is the **honey fungus**, which can kill whole trees. In **Oregon** in the USA, the mycelium of a single **dark honey fungus** stretches over several square kilometres. It is probably several thousand years old.

gewusst: In one gram of forest soil there can be fungal hyphae with a total length of many metres.
Even mould on old bread is made of hyphae.

teile.einleitung: Info Flora is the national data and information centre for the wild plants of Switzerland. It collects observations and shows where which plants occur.
wichtigste: Info Flora collects data on wild plants in Switzerland.
Experts and amateurs can report plant finds.
With the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN), Info Flora produces the Red List of vascular plants.
Invasive neophytes are watched especially closely.
For animals there is info fauna, and for birds the Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach.
All these centres together form the InfoSpecies network.

abschnitte.text: Info Flora collects **data on wild plants** across the whole of Switzerland. Anyone who finds a plant can report the find with place and date. **Experts and amateurs** may do this, for example through an app. From many reports, **distribution maps** are produced. They show where a species occurs and whether it is becoming more common or rarer.

Together with the **Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN)**, Info Flora produces the **Red List of vascular plants**. Vascular plants are plants with conducting tissues, so for example flowers, grasses, trees and ferns. The list shows which species are threatened. That way nature conservation and the authorities know where help is especially needed.

**Neophytes** are plants that have come to us from other continents since the discovery of America. Some spread strongly and **push out native species**. They are called **invasive**. Examples are Japanese knotweed or goldenrod. Info Flora watches these plants especially closely and gives information on how to control them.

Info Flora is not alone. For wild animals there is **info fauna**, and for birds the **Swiss Ornithological Institute** in Sempach. Further centres look after fungi, mosses or lichens. Together they form the **InfoSpecies** network. This produces an overall picture of biodiversity in Switzerland.

gewusst: Every year thousands of new plant reports come in, many of them from volunteers.
Distribution maps also show how plants are shifting because of global warming.

teile.einleitung: Coltsfoot is a small plant with yellow flowers that blooms as early as the very start of spring. It is one of the first signs of spring and likes to grow on bare ground.
wichtigste: Coltsfoot has bright yellow flowers.
It blooms as early as February or March.
The flowers appear before the leaves.
The leaves have the shape of a horse’s hoof.
It is often mistaken for the dandelion.
Its seeds fly on the wind with tiny little parachutes.

abschnitte.text: **Coltsfoot** blooms as early as the **very start of spring**, often from February or March. Its flowers are **bright yellow**. They are among the first yellow flowers of the year. For **bees** and other insects they are an important early food. In dull weather and in the evening, the flowers close.

With coltsfoot, the **flowers** appear first. The large **leaves** only grow later, when the flowering is over. They are round and remind people of the **hoof of a horse**. That is where the name comes from. The underside of the leaves is white and covered in felty hairs.

The flower looks similar to that of the **dandelion**. But coltsfoot blooms earlier and is smaller. A good feature is the **stem**. It is covered with small, reddish **scale leaves**. The dandelion has a smooth, hollow stem and already has leaves when it flowers.

Coltsfoot likes **open, bare ground**. You find it at the **edges of paths**, on **railway embankments**, in gravel pits and on building sites. It is a **pioneer plant** that quickly settles on new ground. Its **seeds** have fine hairs like little **parachutes**. This lets the wind carry them far away.

gewusst: Coltsfoot used to be used as a cough remedy. Because it can contain harmful substances, people nowadays advise against collecting and eating it yourself.
Its scientific name Tussilago means roughly “to drive away a cough”.

teile.einleitung: Japanese knotweed is a very vigorous plant from East Asia. In Switzerland it counts as an invasive neophyte, because it pushes out native plants and causes damage.
wichtigste: Japanese knotweed comes from East Asia.
In the 19th century it came to Europe as an ornamental and fodder plant.
In one summer it can grow up to about 3 metres tall.
Even small pieces of the rootstock can form new plants.
In Europe almost only female plants grow, so there are hardly any seeds able to sprout.
Plant parts belong in the general waste, not on the compost.

abschnitte.text: Japanese knotweed comes from **East Asia**, for example from Japan and China. In the **19th century** it was brought to Europe as an **ornamental and fodder plant**. At that time nobody guessed how strongly it would spread. Today, in Switzerland it is on the list of **invasive neophytes**, that is, introduced plants that cause problems.

In spring, reddish shoots push out of the ground. Within one summer they grow **up to about 3 metres** tall. The stems are **hollow** and resemble bamboo. The plant forms dense stands in which hardly anything else grows. In autumn the parts above ground die off, but the strong **rootstock** in the soil survives.

In Europe almost only **female plants** occur. That is why they hardly form seeds able to sprout here. Even so, the knotweed multiplies very well: even **small pieces of the rootstock** or of the stems can grow into a new plant. They are spread with soil, water or garden waste.

On **stream banks**, the knotweed pushes out native plants with firm roots. In winter the ground beneath it is **bare**, and the water can wear away the bank more easily. This promotes **erosion**. In built-up areas it grows through **cracks in asphalt and walls** and can damage them.

Because even small pieces sprout, plant parts must **not be composted**. They belong **in the general waste**, where they are burned. Control usually takes many years. The plants have to be pulled out or mown again and again until the rootstock is weakened.

gewusst: The rootstock can reach down about two metres into the soil and spread several metres sideways.
In Switzerland it is forbidden to plant or sell Japanese knotweed.

teile.einleitung: How strongly is an animal or plant species threatened with extinction? For this, the International Union for Conservation of Nature, IUCN, has laid down categories that are used worldwide. They are the basis of the Red Lists.
wichtigste: The IUCN was founded in 1948.
Since 1964 it has published the Red List of Threatened Species.
CR, EN and VU together count as “threatened” in the wider sense.
LC means not threatened, and DD means the data are not sufficient.
NE means that a species has not yet been assessed.
Regional Red Lists such as Switzerland’s also have RE.

abschnitte.titel: The International Union for Conservation of Nature
abschnitte.text: The **IUCN** was founded in **1948**. Its seat is in **Gland** in the canton of Vaud, that is, in Switzerland. States, authorities and nature conservation organisations from all over the world belong to it. Since **1964** it has published the **Red List of Threatened Species**. It states how strongly thousands of species are threatened.

Every species gets an abbreviation. **EX** means extinct, **EW** extinct in the wild. Then follow **CR** (critically endangered), **EN** (endangered) and **VU** (vulnerable). These three together count as “threatened” in the wider sense. **NT** means near threatened, **LC** least concern. **DD** means that the data are not sufficient for a classification, and **NE** that a species has not yet been assessed.

Whether a species counts as CR, EN or VU is decided by five **criteria**. Criterion **A** looks at how fast the population is shrinking. If the causes have not been removed, a species counts as CR if it declines by at least **80 per cent** in 10 years or 3 generations. Other criteria look at a small range or very few animals. Criterion **E** is based on a calculation of how likely the species is to die out.

Switzerland also has its own Red Lists, for example for birds, plants or dragonflies. They apply only to the country itself and use the same categories. In addition there is **RE**: a species is extinct in the region but still lives elsewhere. The lists help the authorities to decide where protection is especially urgent.

gewusst: The headquarters of the IUCN is in Switzerland, in Gland on Lake Geneva.
Even a species with many animals can count as threatened if its population is shrinking very quickly.

teile.einleitung: Common ragwort is a wild plant with yellow flowers that grows at the edges of paths and in pastures. It is pretty, but poisonous to horses and cattle.
wichtigste: Common ragwort blooms from about the end of July, around St James’s Day.
Its flowers are bright yellow.
It contains poisons called pyrrolizidine alkaloids.
These poisons damage mainly the liver.
In hay it is especially dangerous, because the bitter taste is missing.
The seeds have white hairs and fly on the wind.

abschnitte.text: The plant blooms from about **St James’s Day** on 25 July, which is where the first part of its German name, “Jakobs-Greiskraut”, comes from. It grows up to about a metre tall and bears many **yellow** flower heads. After flowering, seeds with **white hairs** form. These are reminiscent of the hair of old people, **“Greisenhaar”**. That is why it is called “Greiskraut” in German.

Common ragwort contains **pyrrolizidine alkaloids**. These poisons damage mainly the **liver**. If an animal eats small amounts again and again, the damage builds up. In the pasture, horses and cattle usually avoid the plant because it tastes **bitter**. In **hay** or silage, however, the bitter taste has gone, but the poison has not. That is why the animals then eat it along with the rest.

For the **caterpillar of the cinnabar moth**, the plant is a feast. The caterpillar is conspicuously **ringed in black and yellow**. It takes up the poison and as a result becomes inedible even to birds. The colours warn its enemies. The adult moth has black wings with red spots.

A single plant can produce a great many seeds. These fly off **on the wind** with their hairs. They sprout easily in pastures with gaps in the grass. That is why farmers pull the plants out by the root before the seeds ripen. It is best to wear gloves when doing so.

gewusst: Common ragwort is a native plant and not an introduced neophyte.
The poison can also get into food through honey, if bees collect a lot from the plant.

teile.einleitung: Humus is the dark, fertile part of the soil. It forms from dead plants and animals and is very important for plant growth.
wichtigste: Humus is dark brown to black.
It lies mainly in the topmost layer of soil.
Humus stores water like a sponge.
It contains many nutrients for plants.
Worms, fungi and bacteria turn fallen leaves into humus.
The word “humus” comes from Latin and means earth.

abschnitte.text: **Humus** is an important part of the soil. It makes the earth **fertile** and **loose**. Humus is very dark, **dark brown to black**. The more humus a soil has, the darker it is. The word comes from **Latin** and means earth or ground.

In autumn, leaves fall to the ground, and plants die. **Earthworms**, **woodlice** and other small animals break up the remains. After that, **fungi** and **bacteria** break them down further. In this way humus forms little by little. Because the remains come from above, the **topmost layer of soil** is richest in humus. A thick layer forms only **very slowly**, over many years.

Humus soaks up **water** like a **sponge**. That way plants have water for longer even in dry spells. Humus substances also bind with clay particles and glue soil particles together into small **crumbs**. A crumbly soil is loose and well **aerated**. Roots can grow easily in it.

In humus there are many **nutrients** from rotted plants. The roots of new plants take them up slowly. In this way a **cycle** closes: what once grew becomes food again. That is why gardeners make **compost**. From garden waste and kitchen peelings, humus-rich soil is made.

gewusst: In a handful of good garden soil, there are more living things than there are people on Earth.
Earthworms pull leaves into their burrows and so help to mix the soil.

teile.einleitung: Many flowering plants need insects so that their pollen reaches other flowers. This is called insect pollination. Bees, bumblebees, butterflies and flies are important helpers.
wichtigste: Many flowers reward insects with sweet nectar.
For bees, pollen is a protein-rich food for the larvae.
Honey bees carry pollen in baskets on their back legs.
Around 600 species of wild bee live in Switzerland.
Red clover is pollinated mainly by bumblebees with a long tongue.
Honey bees show with a dance where good flowers are.

abschnitte.text: In **pollination**, pollen passes from one flower to the stigma of another. Only then can seeds and fruits form. Many plants attract insects with colours, scent and **nectar**, a liquid containing sugar. While the insect drinks, pollen sticks to its body. At the next flower it brushes it off again.

Bees also collect **pollen**. It is rich in protein and serves as food for the **larvae**. The **honey bee** carries it home in little “baskets” on its back legs. In Switzerland there are also **around 600 species of wild bee**, which include the bumblebees. In **red clover**, the nectar lies deep in the flower. Only bumblebees with a long tongue can reach it well.

When a honey bee has found a rich source of flowers, she returns to the hive and **dances**. In the so-called waggle dance, the direction of the dance shows where the others should fly. Its length tells how far it is. The researcher Karl von Frisch decoded this bee language.

It is not only bees that pollinate. **Honeysuckle** smells strongly in the evening and is visited mainly by **moths**. Their long tongues reach the nectar in the narrow flower tubes. Some flowers smell of rotting meat and so attract **flies**. They are called **carrion flowers**.

Without insects there would be far fewer apples, cherries, berries and many vegetable seeds. That is why it is important to preserve flower meadows, hedges and nesting places. Every flowering corner of the garden helps the pollinators.

gewusst: In 1973, Karl von Frisch received the Nobel Prize for his research on the language of bees.
Some flowers have patterns that only insects can see, because they perceive ultraviolet light.

teile.einleitung: Humification is the name for the process in which stable humic substances form in the soil from dead plants and animals. It makes the soil dark and fertile and stores a lot of carbon.
wichtigste: In humification, new, stable humic substances form from organic remains.
The opposite process is mineralisation, complete breakdown.
Mull is an active, well-mixed form of humus.
Under acidic conifer forests, raw humus often forms.
Straw has a wide C/N ratio and breaks down slowly.
Soils store more carbon than the atmosphere and plants together.

abschnitte.titel: Building up instead of breaking down
abschnitte.text: When leaves fall or animals die, they are broken down in the soil by living things. One part is broken down completely into **carbon dioxide**, water and mineral salts. This is called **mineralisation**. In the process, nutrients are released again for plants. Another part is converted into new, stable substances, the **humic substances**. This building up is called **humification**.

Humic substances colour the soil **dark** and last a long time. They are classified by their solubility. **Fulvic acids** are relatively small and stay dissolved in acids and alkalis, and they are especially mobile. **Humic acids** dissolve in alkalis but precipitate out in acid. **Humins** are insoluble. An important starting material is **lignin** from wood, which fungi break down only slowly.

Depending on the site, different **forms of humus** arise. **Mull** is very active biologically. Earthworms quickly work the litter in and mix it with the mineral soil. Mull is typical of fertile deciduous woodland and meadow soils. Under acidic **conifer forests**, earthworms are largely absent. Fungi break down the litter slowly, and a thick layer of **raw humus** forms.

How quickly material is broken down depends on the **C/N ratio**, that is, the ratio of carbon to nitrogen. **Cereal straw** contains a lot of carbon and little nitrogen. The microorganisms then lack nitrogen and break it down only slowly. People also distinguish **nutrient humus**, which is broken down quickly and quickly supplies nutrients, from **stable humus**, which lasts for decades to centuries and improves the soil structure.

abschnitte.titel: The soil as a carbon store
abschnitte.text: Worldwide, more **carbon** is bound in the humus of soils than in the **atmosphere** and in all **plants** together. That is why soils play a big part in the climate. When humus is built up, carbon dioxide is taken from the air. When it is broken down, for example when bogs are drained or the soil is worked intensively, carbon dioxide goes into the air.

gewusst: The dark colour of fertile arable soils comes largely from humic substances.
Some humic substances in the soil are hundreds to thousands of years old.

teile.einleitung: The jet stream is a strong band of wind high in the atmosphere. It blows at a height of about 8 to 12 kilometres like an invisible river of air around the Earth. It affects our weather and even how long a flight takes.
wichtigste: The jet stream is a strong band of wind high in the atmosphere.
It usually blows at a height of 8 to 12 kilometres.
The winds often reach more than 200 kilometres per hour.
The jet stream blows around the Earth from west to east.
It arises where warm and cold air masses meet.
It steers high and low pressure areas and thus our weather.
Aeroplanes use it as a tailwind to save fuel.

abschnitte.text: A jet stream is a narrow but very fast **band of strong wind**. It is a few hundred kilometres wide but only a few kilometres thick. It lies just below the **tropopause**, the boundary between the lowest layer of air and the next. You cannot see it, but sometimes long streaks of thin cloud show where it runs.

At the equator the air is warm, at the poles it is cold. Where these air masses meet, a large **temperature difference** arises. This difference and the rotation of the Earth drive the wind at great height towards the east. In this way a **polar front jet stream** forms in each hemisphere, and closer to the equator a subtropical jet stream.

The jet stream does not run dead straight but in large waves and loops around the Earth. These waves are called **Rossby waves**. Sometimes the loops stay in the same place for a long time. Then it can be hot and dry in Europe for weeks, or wet for weeks. In winter the jet stream is usually stronger than in summer, because the temperature differences are greater.

The jet stream steers the **low pressure areas** that move from the Atlantic to Europe. When it lies over central Europe, lows bring wind, cloud and rain to Switzerland. If it shifts northwards, a stable high with sunshine can hold over us. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss therefore watch the jet stream closely.

Many airliners fly at exactly the height at which the jet stream blows. A flight from North America to Europe is often clearly shorter with a **tailwind** than the return flight. Pilots plan their route so that they use the jet stream or avoid it. At the edge of the jet stream, however, it can get bumpy, which is called turbulence.

As early as the 1920s, the Japanese researcher Wasaburo Oishi measured very strong winds at great height with weather balloons. But the jet stream only became well known in the Second World War. At that time American bombers flew so high that they were suddenly slowed down by a huge **headwind**. Today, weather satellites and aeroplanes measure the jet stream every day.

begriffe.erklaerung: The envelope of air that surrounds the Earth.
The boundary between the lowest layer of air, in which the weather happens, and the layer above it.
An area of low air pressure that often brings cloud, wind and rain.
Unsettled, swirling air that can shake an aeroplane.

gewusst: In the core of the jet stream, the wind can reach more than 400 kilometres per hour, faster than a high-speed train.
Because of the jet stream, a flight from New York to Zurich usually takes about an hour less than the flight in the opposite direction.
In 1999, the Swiss Bertrand Piccard and the Briton Brian Jones were the first to fly around the world non-stop in a balloon, carried by jet streams.

teile.einleitung: In hybrid breeding, two different, true-breeding parent lines of a plant are crossed. The first daughter generation, the F1, is often stronger and higher-yielding than both parents.
wichtigste: For hybrids, true-breeding inbred lines are crossed.
The special performance of the F1 is called heterosis.
If you sow seeds from F1 plants, the characteristics split up.
That is why hybrid seed has to be bought again every year.
Hybrid maize greatly raised yields in the USA.
On seed packets, hybrid seed is marked “F1”.

abschnitte.text: First, **inbred lines** are bred. These are plants that have been pollinated only with themselves over several generations and are therefore largely **true-breeding**. If two different inbred lines are crossed, the **F1** results, the first daughter generation. As described by Gregor Mendel’s **law of uniformity**, the F1 plants are very **uniform**. The abbreviation **F1** is also printed on seed packets in the shops.

Often the F1 surpasses both parents in growth and yield. This effect is called **heterosis**. But it is lost in the next generation. If you sow seeds from F1 plants, the characteristics **split up** according to Mendel. The plants become uneven, and the special performance disappears. That is why farmers and gardeners buy **hybrid seed** again every year.

Around **1908**, the researcher **George Harrison Shull** showed with **maize** that inbreeding weakens the plants. Crossing two inbred lines, however, gave strong plants. This laid the foundation for hybrid breeding. In the **USA**, **hybrid maize** took hold from the 1930s. Yields per hectare then rose sharply.

In seed production, the mother line may receive only pollen from the father line. With maize, the **male flower tassels** at the top of the mother plants are removed for this. This is called **detasselling**. It can be done without hand labour using **cytoplasmic male sterility**: such plants do not produce functioning pollen and are therefore only cross-pollinated.

The father of **hybrid rice** is considered to be the Chinese agricultural scientist **Yuan Longping**. In the **1970s** he developed the first high-yielding hybrid rice varieties. As a result, significantly more people could be fed in China from the same area. Today there are also hybrid varieties of vegetables such as tomatoes, cucumbers and cabbage.

gewusst: A large part of the maize grown in Europe and North America today comes from hybrid seed.
If you keep and sow seeds from an F1 tomato, you usually get plants that all look quite different.

teile.einleitung: Seasons are the parts of a year with typical weather, light and temperatures. In Switzerland there are four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter. They arise because the Earth’s axis is tilted relative to the Sun.
wichtigste: In Switzerland there are four seasons.
Winter is followed by spring, and spring by summer.
In autumn, many nuts and apples are ripe.
In winter many plants rest, and it can snow.
Seasons arise because the Earth’s axis is tilted relative to the Sun.
In the Southern Hemisphere the seasons are exactly the other way round.
In the tropics, people distinguish rather between a rainy season and a dry season.

abschnitte.text: The Earth goes around the Sun once in a year. Its **axis** is tilted at an angle of about 23 degrees. In June, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, the Sun stands high and shines for a long time, and then it is summer here. In December, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, the days are short, and it is winter.

In **spring**, the days get longer and warmer, trees put out leaves and many flowers bloom. Migratory birds return, and many animals have young. In summer the days are longest, fields ripen and the grain is harvested. In Switzerland it is then the time for swimming, hiking and the summer on the alpine pastures.

In **autumn**, many fruits ripen, for example apples, pears, grapes and nuts. The deciduous trees turn their leaves colourful and drop them. In winter many plants rest, some animals hibernate, and it can snow. In the Swiss mountains, the winter sports season then begins.

Astronomically, spring begins around 20 March, when day and night are equally long. Summer begins around 21 June with the longest day, the **solstice**. Autumn starts around 22 or 23 September and winter on 21 December with the shortest day. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss calculate more simply and let the seasons begin on 1 March, 1 June, 1 September and 1 December.

In the **Southern Hemisphere**, for example in Australia or Argentina, it is exactly the other way round. When it is winter here, it is summer there, and at Christmas people go swimming. Close to the equator it is warm all year round, and people distinguish a rainy season and a dry season. In the polar regions there is the midnight sun in summer and the polar night lasting months in winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaginary line from the North Pole to the South Pole around which the Earth turns.
The day with the longest or the shortest daylight of the year.
A day in spring or autumn on which day and night are about equally long.
The half of the Earth south of the equator.

gewusst: In January the Earth is actually a little closer to the Sun than in July, so the seasons do not depend on distance.
In Zurich, the longest day of the year is over seven hours longer than the shortest.

teile.einleitung: Honey is a sweet food that bees make from nectar or honeydew. For the bees it is the store for the winter, and for us humans it is a popular spread for bread.
wichtigste: Bees make honey mainly from the nectar of flowers.
Dark forest honey is made from honeydew.
The bees store the honey in the cells of the honeycomb.
Honey is the bees’ winter supply.
The beekeeper gets the honey out of the combs with a honey extractor.
Honey consists mostly of sugar and often turns solid with time.

abschnitte.text: Bees suck **nectar** out of flowers with their tongue. This is a sweet juice. In the hive they pass it on to other bees. These add substances from their bodies and let water evaporate. This makes the juice thicker and it becomes **honey**. Then the bees fill it into the cells of the **honeycomb** and seal them with **wax**.

Honey made from nectar is called **blossom honey**. But there is also **forest honey**. It is darker and stronger in taste. Forest honey is made from **honeydew**. This is a sweet juice that aphids give off on trees such as firs and spruces. The bees collect it in the same way as nectar.

In winter there are no flowers. The bees then stay in the hive and eat their **honey store**. This is how the bee colony survives the cold season. When the beekeeper harvests honey, he has to leave the bees enough food or give them sugar water. Otherwise they would starve in winter.

A person who keeps bees is called a **beekeeper**. He takes the full combs out of the beehive and opens the wax caps. Then he puts the combs into the **honey extractor**. It spins quickly, and the honey sprays out. After that it is strained and filled into jars. Runny honey often turns **solid** with time, because the sugar forms **crystals**. This is quite normal.

gewusst: Honey hardly ever goes off, because it contains very little water and a great deal of sugar.
Honey should not be given to small children under one year old.

teile.einleitung: Jasmonic acid is a plant hormone. It helps plants to defend themselves against enemies that eat them, such as caterpillars. It gets its name from jasmine.
wichtigste: Jasmonic acid is made from the fatty acid alpha-linolenic acid.
Its methyl ester was first found in the fragrant oil of jasmine.
The truly active signal form is jasmonoyl-isoleucine.
Methyl jasmonate is volatile and can warn neighbouring plants.
Wounded tomatoes make proteinase inhibitors via the signal.
Salicylic acid often acts as an opponent of jasmonic acid.

abschnitte.titel: A hormone with a fragrant name
abschnitte.text: **Jasmonic acid** is a **plant hormone**, that is, a messenger substance that passes on signals inside the plant. Its name comes from **jasmine**: in the fragrant oil of this plant, its **methyl ester**, **methyl jasmonate**, was found. Jasmonic acid is made from the fatty acid **alpha-linolenic acid**, which occurs in the cell membranes of plants. The related substances are together called **jasmonates**.

When a caterpillar feeds on a tomato leaf, a small protein is released: **systemin**. In **1991** it was described as the first **peptide hormone** of plants. Systemin triggers the jasmonate defence. The truly active signal form is **jasmonoyl-isoleucine**, a compound of jasmonic acid and a protein building block.

Via the jasmonate signal, the wounded tomato makes **proteinase inhibitors**. These disturb the digestion of the caterpillars, so that they grow worse. The **tobacco plant** makes more **nicotine** after feeding damage, which is poisonous to many insects. In this way the plant protects itself, even though it cannot run away.

**Methyl jasmonate** is **volatile**, so it evaporates into the air. Neighbouring plants can take it up and prepare their defences before an enemy reaches them. Against some disease organisms, by contrast, **salicylic acid** mainly acts. It controls the defence against **biotrophic** pathogens, which live on living tissue. Salicylic acid and jasmonic acid often act as **opponents**.

gewusst: Jasmonic acid occurs in very many plants, not only in jasmine.
Plants can even use volatile substances to attract beneficial insects that eat their enemies.

teile.einleitung: Josias Braun-Blanquet was a botanist from the Grisons. He is regarded as one of the founders of phytosociology, the study of plant communities. His method is still used all over the world today.
wichtigste: Josias Braun-Blanquet was born in Chur in 1884.
In Montpellier he studied under the botanist Charles Flahault.
In 1928 his textbook “Pflanzensoziologie” appeared.
With Eduard Rübel he wrote the “Flora von Graubünden”.
In 1930 he founded the research station SIGMA in Montpellier.
He took the second part of his name, Blanquet, from his wife.

abschnitte.text: Josias Braun was born in **1884** in **Chur**. Even when young he was interested in the plants of the Grisons mountains. In **Montpellier** in southern France he studied under the botanist **Charles Flahault**. He married Gabrielle Blanquet and afterwards called himself **Braun-Blanquet**. So the second part of his name comes from his **wife’s family name**.

Braun-Blanquet noticed that certain plants keep occurring together. Such groups are called **plant communities**. In 1928 his textbook **“Pflanzensoziologie”** appeared. Species that are typical of a community are called **characteristic species**. He arranged the communities into a system. Names of **associations** end in “-etum”, names of **alliances** in “-ion”.

For his method, a **sample plot** is chosen, for example a piece of meadow. All the plant species growing there are written down. For each species, you **estimate** how much area it covers. This **vegetation survey** can be compared with others. That way you can see which communities exist and how they differ.

Together with **Eduard Rübel**, Braun-Blanquet wrote the **“Flora von Graubünden”**. In **1930** he founded the research station **SIGMA** in Montpellier. Experts from many countries worked there. His way of working is also called the Zurich-Montpellier school. He died in 1980 in Montpellier.

gewusst: Braun-Blanquet’s method is still used today in nature conservation and research around the world.
Josias Braun-Blanquet lived to be over 95.

teile.einleitung: Invasive species are introduced plants or animals that spread strongly in a new area and push out native species. Many came to us with trade, as garden plants or as stowaways. In Switzerland, some of them are deliberately controlled.
wichtigste: Invasive species are introduced species that push out native ones.
Plants introduced after 1492 are called neophytes.
In the new area, invasive species often lack their natural enemies.
Common ragweed must be controlled in Switzerland because of its allergenic pollen.
The sap of giant hogweed causes severe skin burns in sunlight.
Since 1 September 2024, cherry laurel may no longer be sold in Switzerland.
Not every introduced species is invasive, and many do no harm.

abschnitte.text: Species that humans have brought into a new area are called **non-native**. Most of them hardly attract attention. But when such a species spreads strongly and causes damage, it counts as **invasive**. It can push out native plants, spread diseases or damage buildings.

In botany, the year 1492, when Columbus reached America, separates old and new arrivals. Plants that came to us before then, such as many arable weeds, are called **archaeophytes**. Plants that were only introduced afterwards are called **neophytes**. From 1492 on, trade and seafaring brought especially many new species across the oceans.

**Himalayan balsam** flings its seeds several metres and forms dense stands on stream banks. Japanese knotweed forms deep rootstocks that can damage bank reinforcements and road surfaces. Giant hogweed grows up to three metres tall, and its sap, together with sunlight, causes severe skin burns. Common ragweed has strongly allergenic pollen and must be reported and controlled in Switzerland.

One important explanation is the **enemy release hypothesis**. It says that in the new area the natural enemies are missing, that is, insects, fungi or diseases that keep the species in check in its home region. In addition, many invasive species grow very quickly and produce many seeds. Climate change also helps some warmth-loving species.

The specialist body Info Flora keeps lists of invasive neophytes in Switzerland. Since 1 September 2024, for example, **cherry laurel**, butterfly bush and tree of heaven may no longer be sold. Municipalities and volunteers pull out invasive plants before they produce seeds. Animals such as the Asian tiger mosquito, the Asian hornet or the quagga mussel in Swiss lakes are also regarded as invasive.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant that was brought into a new area by humans after 1492.
A plant that was introduced by humans before 1492.
A species that already lives naturally in an area.
Animals, fungi or diseases that naturally keep a species in check.

gewusst: Many invasive plants were originally planted in gardens as beautiful ornamental plants.
Parts of invasive neophytes do not belong on the garden compost heap but in the general waste, so that they do not spread further.

teile.einleitung: The Jardin alpin Flore-Alpe is an alpine garden in the Valais. It lies in the mountain village of Champex-Lac and shows plants from mountains all over the world.
wichtigste: The garden lies in Champex-Lac in the canton of Valais.
Champex-Lac belongs to the municipality of Orsières.
It lies at around 1,500 m above sea level on Lac de Champex.
It goes back to a garden by Jean-Marcel Aubert.
The plants come from mountains all over the world.

abschnitte.text: The **Jardin alpin Flore-Alpe** lies in the Valais mountain village of **Champex-Lac**. The village belongs to the municipality of **Orsières** and lies on **Lac de Champex**, at **around 1,500 m above sea level**. People speak **French** here, because the garden is in western Switzerland. “Jardin alpin” means alpine garden. In the cool mountain climate, mountain plants thrive much better than in the lowlands.

The garden from which Flore-Alpe grew was laid out by **Jean-Marcel Aubert**. The plants are shown mainly in **rock gardens** with **rocks and streams**. That way they find conditions similar to those in their home regions, with stony ground and plenty of light. Between the rocks grow small cushion plants, gentians and many other mountain flowers.

abschnitte.titel: Mountain plants from all over the world
abschnitte.text: In the Jardin alpin, it is not only plants from the Alps that grow. They come from **mountains all over the world**, for example from Asia or America. Visitors can thus compare how plants in different mountain regions have adapted to cold, wind and short summers. The garden also serves research and education about the plant life of the mountains.

gewusst: Champex-Lac lies above Orsières, not far from Martigny.
In winter, the snow cover protects alpine plants from frost like a warm blanket.

teile.einleitung: Tree rings are the light and dark rings that you see on a sawn-through tree trunk. Every year a tree grows a new ring. That is why tree rings show the age of the tree and reveal a lot about its life story.
wichtigste: Tree rings show the age of a tree.
Every year a tree forms a new ring.
A tree ring consists of light earlywood and dark latewood.
Wide rings mean good growing years, narrow rings bad ones.
With tree rings, the age of wood can be determined exactly.
In the tropics, many trees have no clear tree rings.

abschnitte.text: Under the bark lies a thin growth layer, the **cambium**. Every year it forms new wood inwards. In spring the tree grows quickly and forms light, loose **earlywood**. In summer growth becomes slower and dark, dense **latewood** forms, and in winter growth rests.

One light and one dark stripe together make a tree ring. If you count all the rings from the centre to the bark, you know how old the tree is. With living trees, a thin borer is used to take out a stick of wood, and the rings on it are counted. That way the tree does not have to be felled.

The width of a ring reveals how the tree was doing in that year. In warm, damp years the rings are wide, in dry or cold years narrow. Scars in the rings show forest fires, lightning strikes or injuries. This is how we learn what the **climate** was like long ago, long before there were weather records.

The science that analyses tree rings is called **dendrochronology**. Because all the trees of an area form wide or narrow rings in the same years, a typical pattern arises. By lining up the patterns of old and young woods, long calendars covering many thousands of years have been made. With them, the year a timber beam was felled can often be determined to the exact year.

In Switzerland, tree rings have been used to date the wooden piles of the **pile dwellings** on lake shores, which have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011. This tells us in which years the villages were built thousands of years ago. The beams of old farmhouses, churches and the Chapel Bridge in Lucerne can also be dated this way. In Birmensdorf near Zurich, the Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research WSL studies tree rings.

begriffe.erklaerung: The thin growth layer under the bark of a tree.
The light, loose wood that grows in spring.
The dark, dense wood that grows in summer.
Determining the age of wood with the help of tree rings.

gewusst: Some bristlecone pines in California are almost 5,000 years old and are among the oldest trees in the world.
Sometimes a tree forms two rings in one year, for example after a frost or a drought in the middle of summer.

teile.einleitung: The International Space Station, or ISS for short, is an inhabited research laboratory in Earth orbit. Since the year 2000, astronauts have lived and worked there all the time. The ISS is the largest structure humans have ever put into space.
wichtigste: The ISS is an inhabited research laboratory in Earth orbit.
It circles the Earth at a height of about 400 kilometres.
One trip around the Earth takes only about an hour and a half.
Since November 2000, the station has been inhabited continuously.
Several space agencies run the ISS together.
You can sometimes see the ISS in the sky with the naked eye.

abschnitte.text: The ISS is a **space station**, that is, a house and laboratory in space. It consists of many modules that were put together like building blocks. With its large solar wings, it is about as wide as a football pitch is long. Electricity is supplied by the **solar cells**, which use sunlight.

The first module was put into space in 1998, and after that the station was extended piece by piece over many years. It is run by the space agencies of the USA, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada. Europe contributed the laboratory module **Columbus**, and Switzerland is a member of the European Space Agency, ESA. Astronauts travel to the station in spacecraft such as Soyuz or Crew Dragon.

The ISS flies at a height of about 400 kilometres at around 28,000 kilometres per hour. It needs only about 90 minutes for one lap of the Earth. That is why the people on board experience about 16 sunrises every day. Because the station is constantly falling around the Earth, there is **weightlessness** on board.

Usually six or seven people live on board for a few months. They research, for example, how plants grow without gravity and how muscles and bones change in space. Such experiments help to prepare future trips to the Moon or to Mars. Every day the astronauts train for about two hours so that their bodies stay fit.

Food comes in pouches and tins, and water is recovered from urine and breath. People sleep in sleeping bags fixed to the wall. In the evening or morning sky, you can see the ISS as a bright, fast-moving point with no blinking light. According to current plans, the station is to be brought down in a controlled way around the year 2030 over a remote part of the **Pacific Ocean**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The path of an object around a heavenly body.
A single building block of the space station.
A state in which you float because you are constantly falling along with everything else.
The European Space Agency, to which Switzerland also belongs.

gewusst: The ISS is so bright that you can often spot it before most of the stars in the evening sky.
There is no shower on the ISS: the astronauts wash with damp cloths and with shampoo that does not need to be rinsed out.

teile.einleitung: The hedgehog is a small mammal with spines. In Switzerland it lives in gardens, hedges and at the edge of woods. It is out and about mainly at night.
wichtigste: An adult hedgehog has about 7,000 spines on its back.
When in danger, it rolls itself into a spiky ball.
It is out and about mainly at night.
It eats mainly beetles, worms and other small animals.
It often sleeps through the winter in a nest of leaves.
Hedges give it shelter and food.

abschnitte.text: On its back the hedgehog carries about **7,000 spines**. They are made of the same material as our hair and fingernails. Its belly and face, by contrast, are covered with soft fur. When danger threatens, the hedgehog rolls itself into a **ball**. Then all the spines point outwards, and many enemies leave it alone.

By day the hedgehog sleeps well hidden. At **dusk and at night** it goes looking for food. In doing so it often walks long distances through several gardens. It has a very good nose and good ears. You often hear it before you see it, because it snuffles and rustles in the leaves.

The hedgehog is an **insect eater**. It eats mainly **beetles**, caterpillars and **earthworms**, but also slugs and millipedes. Milk is unhealthy for hedgehogs, and you should never give it to them. A shallow dish of water, on the other hand, helps them on hot days.

In autumn the hedgehog eats itself a layer of fat. When it gets cold and there is hardly any food left, it goes into **hibernation**. For this it builds a **nest of leaves**, often under a hedge or a pile of branches. Its heart then beats much more slowly, and it needs only a little energy. Only in spring does it wake up again.

A **hedge** is ideal for the hedgehog: it finds **shelter** in it and many insects as food. Leaf piles, wild corners and holes in the garden fence help it too. Roads, robotic lawnmowers and garden poisons are dangerous. Anyone who makes their garden close to nature does the hedgehog a great deal of good.

gewusst: In one night a hedgehog can cover several hundred metres up to a few kilometres.
Young hedgehogs have soft, white spines at first, which only become hard after a while.

teile.einleitung: Evergreen plants bear green leaves or needles all year round. Even in winter you can see them shining green in the woods and in the garden.
wichtigste: Evergreen means that the plant has green leaves all year round.
Evergreen plants also keep losing single old leaves or needles.
A layer of wax protects needles from drying out in winter.
Yew, holly, ivy and box are well-known evergreen plants.
The Swiss stone pine carries its needles in tufts of five, the Scots pine in twos.
The yew is very poisonous in almost all its parts.

abschnitte.text: Many broadleaved trees drop their leaves in autumn. **Evergreen** plants, by contrast, keep them all year round. Even so, their leaves do not last for ever: a **spruce** keeps losing single old needles, which fall off after a few years. Because new ones are constantly growing, the tree stays green. The larch, by the way, is a conifer that drops all its needles in autumn.

In winter the ground is often frozen, and the plant can hardly take up water. That is why needles and hard leaves are well protected. A **layer of wax** on the surface stops them from **drying out**. The narrow shape of the needles also helps to lose little water. In spring, evergreen plants can start making sugar again at once.

With the pines, you can often recognise the species by the tufts of needles. The **Scots pine** has **two** needles together. The **Swiss stone pine**, a tree of the Alps, carries its needles in tufts of **five**. The **yew** has soft, flat needles and red fruits. Its needles and seeds, however, are **very poisonous**, to people and to many animals.

The **holly** has glossy, prickly leaves and red berries. **Ivy** climbs up trees and walls and stays green in winter too. Its berries are winter food for birds, but poisonous for people. The **box** is often clipped into balls or hedges in gardens. Today it suffers in many places from the box tree moth, a moth whose caterpillars eat the leaves.

gewusst: The needles of a spruce often stay on the tree for several years before they fall off.
Ivy only flowers in autumn and is then a late source of food for insects.

teile.einleitung: In hydroponics, plants grow without soil. Their roots stand in water or in a substrate without nutrients, and everything they need they get from a nutrient solution.
wichtigste: Hydroponic plants grow without soil using a nutrient solution.
Indoors, expanded clay is often used as the substrate.
A water level indicator shows when to top up.
In the nutrient film technique, a thin film of nutrient solution flows past the roots.
In aeroponics, the roots are sprayed in the air.
The EC value measures the amount of dissolved nutrient salts.

abschnitte.text: Plants do not actually need soil, but **water**, **air**, **light** and **minerals**. In **hydroponics** they get the minerals from a **nutrient solution**. Around 1860, the researchers **Julius Sachs** and **Wilhelm Knop** grew plants in water cultures with exactly known salts. In this way they proved which minerals plants really need.

For houseplants, **expanded clay** is often used. These are baked, porous **clay pellets**. They give the plant support, store a little water and let air get to the roots. A **water level indicator** with a float shows how much solution is in the pot. When it is at minimum, you add more, but not above optimum, so that the roots get enough air.

In vegetable growing there are larger systems. In the **nutrient film technique**, NFT for short, the plants stand in slightly sloping **channels**. A thin film of nutrient solution flows constantly past the roots. That way they get nutrients and air at the same time. In **aeroponics**, the roots hang freely in a chamber and are sprayed regularly with a fine **mist** of nutrient solution.

Professionals measure their nutrient solution precisely. The **EC value** gives the **electrical conductivity**. Dissolved salts conduct electricity, so the value rises the more nutrient salts are in the solution. The **pH value** is important too. For most plants it is kept at about **5.5 to 6.5**, that is, slightly acidic. Then nutrients such as **iron** and **phosphate** are readily available.

gewusst: With hydroponics, lettuce and herbs can also be grown in buildings, stacked one above the other on shelves.
Expanded clay is made when clay is heated very strongly and puffs up as it does so.

teile.einleitung: In many places today there are clearly fewer insects than in the past. People speak of insect decline. This affects plants, birds and farming too.
wichtigste: The Krefeld study of 2017 showed a sharp fall in insect biomass.
Causes include pesticides, loss of habitat and artificial light.
